newsitem.title: CUBA: In protest, Cuba retracts approval of Spanish envoy.
newsitem.headline: In protest, Cuba retracts approval of Spanish envoy.

text.p: Cuba on Tuesday announced it was retracting its approval for a new Spanish ambassador to the country in protest at what it called Madrid's "flagrant interference in Cuba's internal affairs."

The move, announced by the Foreign Ministry, brought to a head a simmering dispute between Madrid and Havana. Cuba has been increasingly angered by calls from Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government for political change on the communist-ruled island.
Relations between the two countries that have strong historical, cultural and economic ties are at their lowest since a crisis between Madrid and Havana in 1990.

The Foreign Ministry announced the decision on the new ambassador in a lengthy statement published in Tuesday's edition of Communist Party newspaper Granma. The statement listed a series of what it called unacceptable statements and actions by the Aznar government.

It said it was revoking the so-called "placet" (approval) for new ambassador Jose Coderch issued by Havana in October. Coderch had been named by Aznar's government, which took power in May, to replace current ambassador Eudaldo Mirapeix. He had been due to take up his post in early December.

The statement strongly criticized statements on Cuba made in recent weeks by Aznar, Foreign Minister Abel Matutes and Coderch himself. It particularly singled out a plan by Spain to seek to persuade the European Union to adopt a single policy on Cuba following Madrid's line, saying Spain was mimicking United States policy towards the island.
Washington has long maintained an economic embargo on Cuba to try to push President Fidel Castro's government into change.

"Declarations and actions of this type (by Spain) constitute with no doubt at all a flagrant interference in the internal affairs of Cuba and contradict the spirit and letter of the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations," the statement said.

Among its complaints it cited an interview given by Coderch to the Spanish newspaper ABC last month in which he said he intended to have the doors of the Spanish embassy in Havana open to visits by dissidents, saying this attitude was "an open and unacceptable interference in internal affairs".

The statement added Coderch had the "cheek" to suggest that in 1998 -- the 100th anniversary of Cuba's independence from Spain -- Cuba would recover its "so-called freedom". Cuba had waited in vain for a public retraction of these comments, the statement said.

It went on to list statements by Matutes, in which he said Spain sought a "peaceful transition to democracy", and by Aznar, in which he told Castro during a Latin American summit in Chile to "move pieces" as a condition for better relations with Spain.

The ministry also objected to the setting up in Spain earlier this month of a Cuban exile opposition group that includes members of Aznar's ruling Partido Popular (Popular Party) and Miami-based exile leader Jorge Mas Canosa, described in the statement as a "leader of the counter-revolutionary mafia".

It said that it had protested to Spain through diplomatic channels in the hope Madrid would alter its stance. But the Spanish government had continued its attacks in a "rude way". Cuba could not stand passively in the face of this, the statement said.
It added that in removing the placet for the new ambassador, Havana had told the Spanish government of its desire to continue to work to maintain and develop relations with Spain.

Tuesday's move was preceeded by strong statements against the Aznar government by Castro himself. The Cuban leader poured scorn on the Aznar government in comments during a visit to Rome last month, and again criticised the Spanish leader in a speech in Havana at the weekend.
